propositions.text: Applicant seeks judicial review of visa officer's denial of temporary work permit/visa under Temporary Foreign Worker Program.
Visa officer's decision was unreasonable given credible evidence to the contrary.
Disagrees with Applicant's position on unreasonableness of decision.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant seeks judicial review of visa denial, alleging unreasonableness; Respondent disagrees, says decision was reasonable.

propositions.text: Visa officer should have communicated with Applicant to address concerns about visa application.
Disagrees that visa officer should have communicated with Applicant.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant and Respondent disagree whether visa officer should have communicated with Applicant about concerns.

propositions.text: Application for judicial review is allowed for reasons set out below.

paragraphs.summary: Court allows judicial review application for reasons explained below.

propositions.text: Applicant born October 22, 1991, citizen of Nigeria.
Applicant worked as childcare attendant in Nigeria from March 2015 to December 2018.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant is Nigerian born in 1991 and worked as childcare attendant in Nigeria from 2015 to 2018.

propositions.text: Applicant and prospective employer entered into Temporary Foreign Worker Program contract on May 14, 2018.
Contract specified live-in caregiver work for two children in Fort McMurray for 24 months, 44 hours per week.
Applicant's tasks included childcare, light housekeeping, and meal preparation.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant and employer contracted for live-in caregiver work in Fort McMurray for 24 months, 44 hours weekly.

propositions.text: Prospective employer submitted Labour Market Impact Assessment application on May 16, 2018.
On June 19, 2018, Employment and Social Development Canada issued positive LMIA for the position.
LMIA letter stated hiring foreign nationals likely has positive or neutral impact on Canadian labour market.

paragraphs.summary: Employer applied for LMIA in May 2018; positive LMIA issued in June 2018 stating hiring foreign nationals is positive or neutral.

propositions.text: Applicant requested temporary work permit/visa under Program on August 3, 2018, including LMIA number.
Applicant indicated no travel in past five years and did not provide information on assets or funds in application.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant applied for work permit in August 2018, included LMIA number, declared no travel in past five years, no asset info.

propositions.text: Visa officer denied Applicant's temporary work permit/visa application on November 30, 2018.
Applicant did not meet Immigration and Refugee Protection Act and Regulations requirements.
Visa officer not satisfied Applicant will leave Canada based on travel history.
Visa officer not satisfied Applicant will leave Canada based on limited employment prospects in country of residence.
Visa officer not satisfied Applicant will leave Canada based on personal assets and financial status.

paragraphs.summary: Visa officer denied Applicant's work permit, finding Applicant unlikely to leave Canada based on travel history, employment prospects, and finances.

propositions.text: GCMS Notes state Applicant seeks caregiver job for two children under two years old.
Applicant shows no proof of funds/assets or previous travel history.
Applicant currently works in daycare in Nigeria earning approx. $75 Canadian per month.
Visa officer not satisfied Applicant is sufficiently established to motivate return to country of residence.
Application refused for these reasons.

paragraphs.summary: GCMS notes show no proof of funds or travel, low salary, and visa officer refused application for insufficient ties to home country.

propositions.text: Issue 1: Did visa officer act reasonably in denying Applicant's work permit/visa application?
Issue 2: Did visa officer breach procedural fairness by not communicating with Applicant about concerns?

paragraphs.summary: Two issues: reasonableness of visa denial and procedural fairness regarding communication with Applicant.

propositions.text: Reasonableness standard requires decision to be within range of acceptable outcomes defensible on facts and law.
Dunsmuir v New Brunswick defines reasonableness as justified, transparent, and intelligible decision.

paragraphs.summary: Reasonableness standard requires decision to be justified, transparent, and intelligible per Dunsmuir.

propositions.text: Visa officer's discretionary decisions deserve high deference due to factual questions and expertise.
Cites Singh, Portillo, Ngalamulume, Talpur cases supporting deference to visa officers.

paragraphs.summary: Visa officers' discretionary decisions get high deference due to factual nature and expertise, supported by case law.

propositions.text: Visa officers must provide adequate reasons to justify decisions, though minimal duty to provide reasons.
Reasons must allow court to understand decision and assess if within acceptable outcomes (NFLD Nurses, Sibal).

paragraphs.summary: Visa officers must provide adequate reasons enabling court to understand and assess decision's acceptability.

propositions.text: Procedural fairness standard of review is correctness for communication issue.
Cites Lawal, CUPE, Jin, Bahr, Sketchley cases on procedural fairness standard.

paragraphs.summary: Procedural fairness issue reviewed on correctness standard, supported by cited authorities.

propositions.text: Level of procedural fairness owed by visa officer is relaxed due to nature of visa application process.
Cites Zhang and Zhou cases supporting relaxed procedural fairness for visa applications.

paragraphs.summary: Procedural fairness owed by visa officers is relaxed given administrative nature of visa applications.

propositions.text: Visa officer failed to give weight to previous employment and letter of recommendation.
Visa officer misconstrued nature of work permit application.
Visa officer erred in drawing negative inference from lack of travel history.
Visa officer failed to provide sufficient reasons and was not alive to evidence before him.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues visa officer ignored employment history, misconstrued application, erred on travel history, and gave insufficient reasons.

propositions.text: Visa officer considered relevant factors and made reasonable decision.
Visa officer reasonably considered low salary, single status, and economic conditions in Nigeria.
Visa officers not required to provide detailed reasons for decisions.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues visa officer reasonably considered factors and is not required to provide detailed reasons.

propositions.text: Deficiencies in reasons relate closely to reasonableness review (NFLD Nurses).

paragraphs.summary: Deficiencies in reasons are closely linked to reasonableness review per Supreme Court.

propositions.text: Applicants bear burden to rebut presumption they are immigrants and convince officer they will leave Canada.
Cites Danioko, Li, Fakhri Adhari cases on burden of proof for visa applicants.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants must rebut presumption of immigration intent and convince officer they will leave Canada.

propositions.text: Legal presumption: all seeking entry presumed immigrants; applicant must rebut.
Court does not re-weigh evidence in visa decisions.
Officer presumed to have reviewed all evidence unless shown otherwise; no need to reference every document.
Officer's reasons include form, letter, and GCMS notes.

paragraphs.summary: Presumption of immigrant intent applies; court does not re-weigh evidence; officer presumed to review all evidence; reasons include form, letter, GCMS notes.

propositions.text: Visa officer denied visa because Applicant failed to show she would leave Canada after work contract
Decision based on Applicant's lack of funds, no travel history, and poor employment prospects in Nigeria

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker denied the Applicant's visa due to lack of funds, travel history, and poor employment prospects, doubting she would leave Canada after work.

propositions.text: Visa officers commonly use templates for efficiency
Visa officers have wide discretion and may consider objective criteria
Visa officers' discretion and use of objective criteria supported by Zhang and Zhou cases

paragraphs.summary: The court finds visa officers commonly use templates and have wide discretion, supported by prior cases Zhang and Zhou.

propositions.text: Visa officers using templates must modify reasons intelligibly and address contradictory evidence
Visa officer here failed to explain how evidence was interpreted to reach decision

paragraphs.summary: The court states visa officers must explain reasoning intelligibly and address contradictory evidence; here, the visa officer failed to do so.

propositions.text: Visa officer's reasons are hurried and lack explanation of thought process
Decision incorrectly references study permit legislation instead of work permit legislation
This error suggests inattention but is not fatal as GCMS notes align with work permit criteria

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the visa officer's reasons hurried with a legislative reference error, but this is not fatal given GCMS notes alignment.

propositions.text: The Decision has several shortcomings

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Decision suffers from several shortcomings.

propositions.text: Visa officer failed to give sufficient weight to Applicant's reasonable employment history in Nigeria
GCMS notes mention Applicant's daycare employment and positive recommendation
Applicant has training certificates and over three years employment in Nigeria
These factors could displace finding of poor employment prospects
Visa officer should have specifically addressed Applicant's employment history given its significance

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the visa officer failed to consider Applicant's positive employment history and related evidence adequately.

propositions.text: Visa officer drew negative inference from Applicant's salary without context
GCMS notes state Applicant earns approx. $75 Canadian per month
No explanation if salary suffices for reasonable living standard in Nigeria
Visa officers may use general knowledge but must contextualize salary evidence

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the visa officer negatively inferred from salary without contextualizing its adequacy for living standards in Nigeria.

propositions.text: Better job prospects in Canada common for applicants from lower living standard countries
Visa officer's failure to address stable employment history and salary context undermines justification and intelligibility

paragraphs.summary: The court finds visa officer's failure to address employment history and salary context undermines decision's justification and intelligibility.

propositions.text: Visa officer cited Applicant's limited funds as reason to deny visa without mentioning job offer in Canada
No explanation on how job offer affects sufficiency of funds criterion

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the visa officer failed to consider Applicant's Canadian job offer when citing limited funds as a denial reason.

propositions.text: Further comment on funds not needed for study permits but needed for work permits like this case

paragraphs.summary: The court finds further comment on funds is necessary for work permit cases like this one, unlike study permits.

propositions.text: Lack of travel history should be treated as neutral factor for work permit applicants' return likelihood
Federal Court cases Ogunfowora, Huang, Adom support treating lack of travel history as neutral

paragraphs.summary: The court states lack of travel history is a neutral factor for return likelihood, supported by prior Federal Court cases.

propositions.text: Visa officer erred by using Applicant's lack of travel history as negative factor for return

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the visa officer erred by treating Applicant's lack of travel history negatively in return assessment.

propositions.text: Visa officer has discretion to assign weight to evidence
Visa officer should have articulated reasons to allow court to assess justification, transparency, intelligibility
Singh case requires reasons to fit principles of justification, transparency, intelligibility

paragraphs.summary: The respondent argues discretion in weighing evidence; the court finds reasons should be articulated per Singh principles.

propositions.text: Visa officer was not attuned to nature and content of Applicant's work permit application
Court understands visa officer's points but not reasons; understanding reasons is important

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the visa officer misunderstood the application and failed to explain reasons clearly, which is important.

propositions.text: Visa officer should have called Applicant to address concerns before rejection, citing Wang case

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues the visa officer should have contacted her to address concerns before refusal, citing Wang.

propositions.text: Visa application process has relaxed duty of fairness due to volume and nature of visa applications
Khan case explains limited duty of fairness due to no legal right to visa and burden on applicant
Khan cautions against procedural formality that impedes efficient visa administration

paragraphs.summary: The court explains visa process has relaxed fairness duty, supported by Khan case citing no legal visa right and efficiency concerns.

propositions.text: Additional communication appropriate if doubts about credibility, extrinsic evidence, or stereotypes arise
Salman and Hassani cases support additional communication in such circumstances

paragraphs.summary: The court states additional communication may be needed if credibility or extrinsic evidence doubts arise, supported by Salman and Hassani.

propositions.text: Wang case found visa officer should have allowed Applicant to respond to concerns about sincerity and bona fides

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Wang found visa officer should have allowed Applicant to respond to sincerity and bona fides concerns.

propositions.text: Visa officer must inform Applicant when relying on extrinsic evidence for decision
Ali case supports informing Applicant of extrinsic evidence use

paragraphs.summary: The court states visa officers must inform Applicants when extrinsic evidence is used, per Ali case.

propositions.text: Visa officers may not rely on cultural or regional generalizations without allowing Applicant to respond
Yuan and Hernandez Bonilla cases support this principle

paragraphs.summary: The court states visa officers cannot rely on cultural generalizations without Applicant response, supported by Yuan and Hernandez Bonilla.

propositions.text: This Court has consistently rejected the argument that an applicant has the right to clarify or respond to the visa officer's decision.
Ling v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2003 FC 1198 at para 16 supports this rejection.
Li; Wen v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2002 FCT 1262 also supports this rejection.

paragraphs.summary: The court states it has consistently rejected applicants' right to clarify or respond to visa officer decisions, citing Ling and Li; Wen cases.

propositions.text: The present case does not fall within exceptions requiring heightened duty of fairness.
No evidence suggests the visa officer doubted the applicant's credibility, veracity, or sincerity.
No evidence that the visa officer relied on broad generalizations about the applicant or country of origin.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no exceptions apply and no evidence of visa officer doubting applicant's credibility or relying on generalizations.

propositions.text: The visa officer did not err by not providing the applicant an opportunity to further justify her visa application.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the visa officer did not err in denying the applicant further justification opportunity.

propositions.text: The visa officer did not provide a sufficiently clear indication of the basis for his decision.
The reasons given fail to allow determination if the conclusion is within acceptable outcomes.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the visa officer's reasons are unclear and insufficient to determine if the decision is acceptable.

propositions.text: The application for judicial review is allowed.
The visa officer's decision is set aside.
The matter is remitted to a different officer for redetermination.
No certified question was submitted or arose.

paragraphs.summary: The court allows judicial review, sets aside visa officer's decision, remits matter for redetermination, and notes no certified question.
